Compare the candidate with each remaining string from left to right.
When a mismatch or end of a string is reached, shorten the candidate to the matched portion.
If the candidate becomes empty, the answer is immediately "".
title: Maximum-Length Common Prefix

notes: Return the longest prefix common to all strings in the input array.
If any string is empty, the result is the empty string.
The input may contain digits and lowercase letters; matching is exact and case-sensitive.
A straightforward approach is to use the first string as a reference and compare characters position-by-position across all other strings.
constraints: Each non-empty strs[i] contains only lowercase English letters and digits (characters in [a-z0-9]).
Expected time complexity: O(n * m); expected extra space: O(m).
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array containing one array of strings: [["str1","str2",...]]. Example: [["flower","flow","flight"]]
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialized string representing the longest common prefix, e.g. "fl"

sampleTestCases.explanation: The longest prefix common to all three strings is "fl".
The strings have no common starting character, so the longest common prefix is empty.

content.problemStatement:
Write a function that returns the longest common prefix string shared among an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, output an empty string "".

The longest common prefix is the longest string that is a prefix of every string in the input array. The function should be case-sensitive and treat digits and lowercase letters as distinct characters.

Design an algorithm that runs in O(n * m) time where n is the number of strings and m is the length of the common prefix, and uses O(m) extra space for the result.

notes: Hidden tests cover minimum and maximum string counts, empty strings, duplicate-heavy inputs, alphanumeric matching, and 200-character boundary cases.
All expected outputs are exact JSON string equality comparisons.
Whitespace around the output line is trimmed by the harness before comparison.
The algorithm uses the current prefix as the only working state and stops immediately after the first mismatch.
solution.approach: Use the first string as the current prefix. For each remaining string, compare characters from the beginning until either string ends or a mismatch occurs, then shorten the current prefix to the matching portion. If the prefix becomes empty, stop early. The final prefix is common to every string.

better.complexity: O(n * m) time and O(m) space for the returned prefix.
better.description: Use the first string as a reference and compare each character position across all strings. Stop at the first mismatch or when any string ends.

optimal.complexity: O(n * m) time and O(m) space for the result.
optimal.description: Maintain a current common prefix and shrink it while scanning the remaining strings. Each character that remains in the prefix is validated against the other strings, and the scan stops immediately when no common prefix remains.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n * m^2) in the worst case because multiple candidate prefixes may be checked.
bruteForce.description: Check every possible prefix of the first string, starting from the longest, and test whether it is a prefix of every other string. Stop at the first valid prefix.

followUps: Can you solve it by sorting the strings first? What trade-off does sorting introduce?
Can the solution be implemented using a trie? Compare its time and space costs with the direct comparison approach.
How would the solution change if uppercase letters or Unicode characters were allowed?

Handle empty strings, unequal lengths, duplicates, and alphanumeric characters correctly.
